question: A switch described as 'single-pole, double-throw' (SPDT):

options.text: Connects one input to either of two outputs
Connects two separate inputs to one common output at the same time
Switches two independent circuits on or off together with one lever
Opens or closes a single circuit only, with one on and one off position

explanation: 'Pole' is the number of separate circuits the switch controls; 'throw' is the number of positions each pole can connect to. SPDT is one circuit routed to one of two destinations — a changeover switch.

question: A double-pole, single-throw (DPST) switch is used when:

options.text: A circuit must be opened before a second circuit is made
A circuit must be made momentarily and then released automatically
Two separate circuits must be made or broken together by one operation
One circuit must be routed to either of two different loads

explanation: Two poles mean two electrically separate circuits; single throw means each is simply on or off. Both change state together — for example breaking both the supply and the return lead of a two-wire circuit.

question: A 'break-before-make' changeover switch is designed so that:

options.text: The old connection opens before the new one closes, so two supplies are never joined
The contacts open automatically if the current exceeds a set value
The new connection closes before the existing one opens, so the load is never without supply
The switch cannot be operated while current is flowing through it

explanation: Break-before-make guarantees there is no instant at which both positions are connected — essential where joining the two sources would cause a short circuit or an unwanted paralleling. Make-before-break does the opposite to avoid interrupting a load.

question: A microswitch is characterised by:

options.text: Contacts that only ever carry microamp signal currents
A tiny actuator movement gives a fast, positive snap action of the contacts
Operation by a magnetic field, with no physical contact needed
A large lever travel needed to separate the contacts slowly and quietly

explanation: A spring 'snap' mechanism means a tiny movement of the plunger changes the contacts over quickly, regardless of how slowly it is pressed. That makes microswitches ideal for sensing positions — flap, door, gear and throttle positions.

question: Proximity switches are often preferred to mechanical microswitches for landing gear and door position sensing because they:

options.text: Can carry the full motor current of the landing gear actuator directly
Need no electrical supply, because they generate their own signal
Can only detect steel targets, which prevents false indications
Have no exposed moving contacts, so dirt, ice and wear affect them less

explanation: A proximity sensor detects a target (typically by its effect on an inductive or magnetic field) without touching it, so there is nothing to jam, bounce or wear. Its output usually feeds an electronic unit rather than switching heavy loads directly.

question: A guarded switch in the cockpit is fitted to:

options.text: Allow the switch to be operated only when the aircraft is on the ground
Stop a critical function being selected by accident
Protect the switch from overcurrent by adding a fuse inside the guard
Hold the switch in the on position permanently once it has been selected

explanation: A guard is purely a mechanical barrier against inadvertent selection of items such as fire handles, generator disconnects or battery switches. It has no electrical function.

question: A thermal (temperature-sensitive) switch commonly uses:

options.text: A bimetal element that bends with temperature to operate the contacts
A diode whose forward voltage drop opens the contacts at a set temperature
A capacitor that discharges through the contacts when a set temperature is reached
A coil whose magnetic field strengthens with temperature and pulls in an armature

explanation: Two metals with different expansion coefficients bonded together bend as they warm. That movement operates the contacts — used in overheat detection, motor protection and thermal circuit breakers.

question: The main purpose of a relay is to:

options.text: Allow a small control current to switch a much larger load current at a distance
Step a supply voltage up or down to suit a particular load
Convert a direct current into an alternating current for a remote load
Protect a circuit by opening automatically when its current becomes excessive

explanation: A relay is an electrically operated switch. A light cockpit switch and thin wiring energise the relay coil; the relay's own heavy contacts, placed close to the load, carry the large current. This saves weight and keeps heavy current out of the cockpit.

question: When the coil of a normally open relay is de-energised:

options.text: Its contacts are open and the controlled circuit is broken
Its contacts stay in whatever position they were last in
Its contacts vibrate continuously until the coil is energised again
Its contacts are closed and the controlled circuit is made

explanation: 'Normally' describes the relaxed, de-energised state. A normally open relay's spring holds its contacts apart until the coil current pulls the armature in. A normally closed relay is the reverse.

question: A latching (mechanically or magnetically held) relay differs from an ordinary relay in that:

options.text: It can only switch alternating current loads
It stays in its last position after the pulse ends, until it is reset
It returns to its normal position the moment the coil current is removed
It needs a continuous holding current to keep its contacts closed

explanation: A latching relay needs only a brief pulse to change state and none to stay there. It is useful where a position must be remembered through a power interruption, and it saves the holding current an ordinary relay would draw.

question: A polarised relay is one which:

options.text: Contains a diode that keeps its contacts closed after the coil is de-energised
Operates only when its coil current flows in one particular direction
Operates whenever its coil current exceeds a set value, in either direction
Operates on alternating current but not on direct current

explanation: A permanent magnet in the magnetic circuit means the armature responds to the direction of the coil's field, not only its strength. This makes the relay sensitive to the polarity of the signal — used, for example, in reverse-current sensing.

question: Why is a diode often connected across the coil of a DC relay?

options.text: To increase the current through the coil and make the relay close faster
To keep the relay energised briefly after the control switch is opened
To absorb the high voltage induced by the collapsing field when the coil is switched off
To allow the relay to operate on alternating current as well as direct current

explanation: A coil opposes any change in its current. When the supply is broken, the collapsing field induces a large back-EMF that can arc across the switch or damage electronics. A reverse-biased 'suppression' diode gives that energy a harmless path.

question: Compared with a relay, a solenoid (contactor) used in heavy-current circuits typically has:

options.text: A bimetal strip that closes the contacts as the coil warms up
A permanent magnet armature that latches its contacts with no coil at all
Very fine contacts designed for signal currents of a few milliamps
A soft-iron plunger drawn into the coil, working heavy-current contacts

explanation: In a solenoid the coil pulls a soft-iron core into its centre, giving a long, powerful stroke. That is what makes it suitable for the battery, ground power and starter contactors, where hundreds of amps must be switched.

question: The starter of an engine draws a very heavy current. The cockpit start switch therefore normally:

options.text: Closes the battery master switch, which then carries the starter current
Carries the full starter current directly through its own contacts
Energises a starter solenoid, whose contacts carry the starter current
Connects the starter to the supply through a resistor that limits the current

explanation: The cockpit switch only carries the small coil current. The solenoid, mounted close to the battery and starter, carries the hundreds of amps — short heavy cables and a light switch, instead of heavy cables run to the cockpit.

question: The pull of a relay or solenoid coil on its armature depends mainly on:

options.text: The voltage of the supply alone, whatever current flows
The frequency of the supply, even on a DC coil
Its ampere-turns: coil current multiplied by number of turns
The resistance of the contacts it is switching

explanation: Magnetising force is proportional to current × turns. More turns or more current give a stronger field and a stronger pull; the iron core and the size of the air gap then determine how much flux that force produces.

question: A relay whose contacts are rated for 5 A is used to switch a 15 A load. The most likely result is:

options.text: No effect, because contact ratings apply only to AC loads
The relay refusing to close, because the load current opposes the coil field
Arcing and overheating of the contacts, leading to pitting or welding together
The relay coil drawing three times its rated current and burning out

explanation: Contact ratings are set by the heat and arcing the contacts can tolerate when making, carrying and breaking current. Overloading them erodes the contact faces and can weld them closed, so the circuit can no longer be switched off. The coil is unaffected.

question: Switch contacts that switch an inductive load such as a motor are prone to arcing when they open because:

options.text: The motor generates alternating current that cannot be interrupted
The inductance induces a high voltage as the current is forced to fall
The current through an inductive load is always greater than its rated value
The contacts are cooled by the motor's airflow and lose their resistance

explanation: Any inductance resists a change in current. Opening the circuit tries to stop the current instantly, so a large self-induced EMF appears across the gap and can ionise the air into an arc. That is why inductive-load switches are de-rated or fitted with suppression.

question: A time-delay relay is used in an aircraft circuit to:

options.text: Limit the current in a circuit to a safe value for a set time
Measure how long a circuit has been energised for maintenance records
Reverse the polarity of a circuit at regular timed intervals
Switch a circuit a set time after its control signal changes

explanation: Time-delay relays introduce a deliberate pause — for example letting a pump reach speed before another load is connected, or ignoring a momentary signal before triggering a warning.

question: Switches in a DC circuit are normally fitted in the positive (supply) lead rather than the earth return because:

options.text: Earth-return leads are not permitted to carry current through a switch
The current in the positive lead is larger than in the return lead
A switch in the return lead would reverse the direction of current in the load
When open, the load and its wiring are then dead and safe to work on

explanation: Switching the return leaves the load connected to the live supply even when 'off', so a chafed wire downstream can still short to structure. Breaking the live side removes voltage from everything after the switch.

question: A relay coil is designed for 28 V DC. If it is operated from a bus that has fallen to 18 V, the most likely effect is that the relay:

options.text: Operates normally, because relay operation is independent of supply voltage
Pulls in more strongly, because a lower voltage draws a larger current
Overheats and burns out, because the coil current rises at low voltage
May fail to pull in or may chatter, because the coil's ampere-turns are reduced

explanation: At lower voltage a fixed coil resistance draws less current, giving fewer ampere-turns and a weaker pull. Below its pick-up value the relay may not close, or may close and drop out repeatedly (chatter) — one reason a low bus voltage produces odd, intermittent faults.
